slides.narration: A constitution is written once, but a country goes on changing. How can a constitution stay faithful to its first principles and still meet new needs? In this part we study why the Indian Constitution can be amended, the three ways in which it is changed, the rules of the procedure, and the kinds of amendments that have been made.

slides.heading: Why a constitution must be able to change

rows: Why a constitution changes
Society, needs and knowledge change, so a constitution must be able to adapt
Rigid constitution
One that is difficult to change, because change needs a demanding procedure
Flexible constitution
One that can be changed easily, in the way an ordinary law is changed
The Indian balance
Some parts can be changed easily, most need a special majority, and some also need the states

visual.alt: Table on why constitutions change: society and needs change so a constitution must adapt; a rigid constitution is difficult to change; a flexible constitution can be changed easily like an ordinary law; the Indian Constitution strikes a balance, with some parts changed easily, most needing a special majority, and some also needing the states

slides.narration: A constitution must be able to change because society and its needs change. A rigid constitution is difficult to change, because change needs a demanding procedure. A flexible constitution can be changed easily, in the way an ordinary law is changed. The Indian Constitution strikes a balance between the two.

slides.heading: Article 368 and the three ways

rows: What it provides
The power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and the procedure for doing so
Three ways, as commonly taught
A simple majority; a special majority; a special majority with ratification by the states
Who can start it
An amendment bill may be introduced in either House of Parliament
Where the bill is passed
In each House separately, because there is no joint sitting for amendment bills

visual.alt: Table on Article 368: it gives the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and the procedure; three ways are commonly taught, a simple majority, a special majority, and a special majority with ratification by the states; a bill may be introduced in either House and is passed in each House separately because there is no joint sitting

slides.narration: Article three hundred and sixty eight gives Parliament the power to amend the Constitution and lays down the procedure. As commonly taught, there are three ways of changing the Constitution. The first is a simple majority, the second a special majority, and the third a special majority with ratification by the states.

visual.caption: The three ways of changing the Constitution.

slides.narration: This chart sets the three methods side by side. The first is an ordinary law, used for forming new states and for Legislative Councils. The second is a special majority in each House, used for most provisions, including the Fundamental Rights. The third adds ratification by the states, and is used for federal matters. For all of them, either House may start the bill, and the President must assent.

slides.heading: Way one: the simple majority

rows: How it is passed
As an ordinary law, by a simple majority of members present and voting
Article 3
Forming new states, and changing the area, boundaries or names of states
Article 169
Creating or abolishing a Legislative Council in a state, after a resolution of the state Assembly
Status
Technically not counted as amendments under Article 368

visual.alt: Table on the simple majority: such a change is passed as an ordinary law by a simple majority of members present and voting; examples are Article 3 on forming new states and changing boundaries or names, and Article 169 on creating or abolishing a Legislative Council after a resolution of the state Assembly; technically these are not counted as amendments under Article 368

slides.narration: Some changes are made as an ordinary law, by a simple majority of members present and voting. Article three allows Parliament to form new states and to change their area, boundaries or names. Article one hundred and sixty nine allows a Legislative Council to be created or abolished in a state. Technically, these are not counted as amendments under Article three hundred and sixty eight.

slides.heading: Way two: the special majority

rows: Condition 1
A majority of the total membership of the House
Condition 2
Two thirds of the members present and voting
Both needed
A bill that meets only one of the two conditions fails
Used for
Most provisions of the Constitution, including the Fundamental Rights

visual.alt: Table on the special majority: a majority of the total membership of the House, and two thirds of the members present and voting; both are needed, and a bill meeting only one fails; it is used for most provisions including the Fundamental Rights

slides.narration: A special majority has two conditions. First, a majority of the total membership of the House. Second, two thirds of the members present and voting. Both are needed, and a bill that meets only one of them fails. Most provisions of the Constitution, including the Fundamental Rights, are amended in this way.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: counting the votes
slides.body_md: An imagined House has five hundred and forty members in total. Test two outcomes of a vote on an imagined amendment bill.

headers: Imagined House with 540 members in total
rows: The imagined bill
The 140th Amendment Bill, to widen a Fundamental Right
Condition 1
More than half of 540 means at least 271 votes for the bill
Condition 2
With 360 present and voting, two thirds is 240 votes
Case A: 300 vote for
300 is at least 271 and at least 240: the bill passes in this House
Case B: 270 vote for
270 is above 240 but below 271: the bill fails

visual.alt: Worked example table on counting votes in an imagined House of 540 members: the imagined 140th Amendment Bill needs at least 271 votes for condition one and, with 360 present and voting, 240 for condition two; in case A, 300 votes pass the bill, and in case B, 270 votes fail it because 270 is below 271
visual.caption: The bill, the House and all numbers are imagined.

slides.narration: Imagine a House with five hundred and forty members in total. More than half means at least two hundred and seventy one votes. With three hundred and sixty members present and voting, two thirds is two hundred and forty. If three hundred vote for the bill, both conditions are met. If only two hundred and seventy vote for it, the second condition is met but the first is not, so the bill fails.

slides.heading: Way three: ratification by the states

rows: Election of the President
The states take part in the election
Executive power of the Union and the states
It concerns the division of power between the two levels
The Supreme Court and the High Courts
The courts serve the Union and the states
Lists of the Seventh Schedule
They divide subjects between the Union and the states
Representation of states in Parliament
It concerns how states are heard at the centre
Article 368 itself
The way of amending must not be changed without the states

visual.alt: Table of the matters needing ratification by at least half of the state legislatures: the election of the President, the executive power of the Union and the states, the Supreme Court and the High Courts, the lists of the Seventh Schedule, the representation of states in Parliament, and Article 368 itself, each affecting the federal structure

slides.narration: Some matters affect the federal structure. These are the election of the President, the executive power of the Union and the states, the Supreme Court and the High Courts, the lists of the Seventh Schedule, the representation of states in Parliament, and Article three hundred and sixty eight itself. For these, the special majority is not enough. At least half of the state legislatures must also ratify the amendment.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: which method applies?
slides.body_md: Four imagined bills are before Parliament. Match each with the correct method.
bullets: Is it an **ordinary law** under Article 3?

rows: A law forming the imagined state of Tarnia from districts of Merivia
Simple majority under Article 3; not an amendment under Article 368
The 140th Amendment Bill: widen a Fundamental Right
Special majority in each House; no ratification by the states
The 141st Amendment Bill: move a subject from the State List to the Union List
Special majority plus ratification by at least half of the states
The 142nd Amendment Bill: change the way the President is elected
Special majority plus ratification; the election of the President is a federal matter

visual.alt: Worked example table sorting imagined bills by method: a law forming the imagined state of Tarnia from districts of Merivia needs a simple majority under Article 3; the 140th Amendment Bill on widening a Fundamental Right needs a special majority without ratification; the 141st Amendment Bill moving a subject between lists needs a special majority plus ratification; the 142nd Amendment Bill on the election of the President needs a special majority plus ratification
visual.caption: All the bills and the state are imagined.

slides.narration: Let us sort four imagined bills. A law forming the imagined state of Tarnia needs a simple majority under Article three. A bill to widen a Fundamental Right needs a special majority, without ratification. A bill to move a subject from the State List to the Union List needs the special majority and ratification by the states. A bill to change the way the President is elected also needs ratification, because it is a federal matter.

slides.heading: Other rules of the procedure

rows: Where it starts
In either House of Parliament; a state legislature cannot begin it
Joint sitting
None for amendment bills: each House must pass the bill on its own
Assent
The President must give assent; the 24th Amendment (1971) made this obligatory
How many amendments
More than one hundred; the 106th, in 2023, is the latest as of 2024

slides.narration: This timeline brings together the landmarks. The Constitution came into force in nineteen fifty. The retirement age of judges was changed in nineteen sixty three. slides.narration: A Constitution lives not only through amendments. Courts explain what a provision means and, over time, can read a wider meaning into it. sections.heading: 1. Why a constitution is amended
sections.body_md: A constitution is written at one time but has to serve later times, so it needs a way of changing. A **rigid constitution** is hard to change; a **flexible constitution** can be changed as easily as an ordinary law. The Indian Constitution is a **balance** of the two: some parts are changed easily, most need a special majority, and some need the states as well.

A constitution that is difficult to change, because change needs a demanding procedure.
A constitution that can be changed easily, in the way an ordinary law is changed.

sections.heading: 2. Article 368: the three ways
sections.body_md:
**Article 368** gives Parliament the power to amend the Constitution and lays down the procedure. As commonly taught, there are three ways:

- **Simple majority:** ordinary laws, such as **Article 3** (new states) and **Article 169** (Legislative Councils), technically not amendments under Article 368.
- **Special majority in each House:** for most provisions, including the **Fundamental Rights**.
- **Special majority plus ratification by at least half of the state legislatures:** for federal matters.

key_terms.definition_md: More than half of the members present and voting.
A majority of the total membership of a House together with two thirds of the members present and voting.
Formal approval of an amendment by the legislatures of the states, where the Constitution requires it.

sections.heading: 3. Federal matters and the rules of the procedure
sections.body_md:
The matters that need ratification include the **election of the President**, the **executive power of the Union and the states**, the **Supreme Court and the High Courts**, the **lists of the Seventh Schedule**, the **representation of states in Parliament** and **Article 368** itself.

A bill can start in **either House**; there is **no joint sitting**; the **President must assent** (24th Amendment, 1971). More than a hundred amendments have been made; the 106th, in 2023, is the latest as of 2024.

key_terms.definition_md: A provision that affects the division of power between the Union and the states; amending it needs ratification by the states.

sections.heading: 4. Kinds of amendments and the 1970s
sections.body_md:
Amendments are commonly grouped as **technical or administrative** (15th, 1963: retirement age of High Court judges from 60 to 62), those from **differing interpretations** of the judiciary and Parliament, those through **political consensus** (52nd, 1985; 61st, 1988; 73rd and 74th, 1992) and the **controversial amendments of the 1970s**.

The **42nd Amendment (1976)** was passed during the national Emergency (1975 to 1977); it changed many parts of the Constitution, added socialist, secular and integrity to the Preamble and added the Fundamental Duties. The **44th Amendment (1978)** restored several provisions.

sections.heading: 5. The basic structure doctrine
sections.body_md:
**Golaknath (1967):** Parliament cannot amend the Fundamental Rights. **24th Amendment (1971):** Parliament asserted its power over every part. **Kesavananda Bharati (1973):** Parliament can amend any part but **cannot alter the basic structure**. **Minerva Mills (1980):** the doctrine was reaffirmed, with the balance between the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles.

The courts have identified features over time, for example: supremacy of the Constitution, the republican and democratic form of government, the secular character, separation of powers, the federal character, judicial review and the rule of law.

key_terms.definition_md: The core features of the Constitution that Parliament cannot alter by amendment, as identified by the courts.
The power of the courts to examine whether laws and amendments follow the Constitution and to strike down those that do not.
The rights in Part III of the Constitution that citizens can enforce in the courts.
Guidelines in Part IV of the Constitution for governments in making policy, which the courts do not enforce.

sections.heading: 6. Significance of the doctrine
sections.body_md:
The doctrine **balances rigidity and flexibility**: the wide amending power gives flexibility, and the protection of the core gives stability. It **limits the amending power**.

**Some argue** that it gives judges too much power over an elected Parliament. **Others argue** that it protects the core of the Constitution from a passing majority. A good answer presents both and gives reasons.

Elected representatives should have the last word on amendments
Some features are so central that no majority should change them

sections.heading: 7. The Constitution as a living document
sections.body_md: A **living document** grows with society and keeps its core. It changes through **amendments** by Parliament, through **judicial interpretation** (courts have read the right to livelihood and the right to privacy into **Article 21**) and through **political practice and conventions**. Parliament and the judiciary contribute together.

An accepted practice, not written in a law, that guides how political actors behave and fills a silence in the text.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Saying every change needs a special majority: Article 3 and Article 169 changes need only a simple majority.
- Defining the special majority as two thirds of the total membership: it is a majority of the total membership and two thirds of those present and voting.
- Saying a joint sitting settles a deadlock on an amendment bill: there is no joint sitting for amendment bills.
- Saying Kesavananda Bharati stopped all amendments: Parliament can amend any part but cannot alter the basic structure.
- Taking a side on the doctrine without reasons: present both views.

**Tips:** put the cases in order with years (1967, 1971, 1973, 1980); give one example for each method; use imagined bills and countries for examples; date facts (the 106th Amendment, 2023, as of 2024).

cards.front_md: Why does a constitution need an amendment procedure?
cards.back_md: So that it can adapt to new needs and still stay stable.

cards.front_md: What is a **rigid** constitution?
cards.back_md: One that is difficult to change, because change needs a demanding procedure.

cards.front_md: What is a **flexible** constitution?
cards.back_md: One that can be changed easily, in the way an ordinary law is changed.

cards.front_md: Which Article lays down the amendment procedure?
cards.back_md: Article 368.

cards.front_md: Name the three ways of changing the Constitution
cards.back_md: A simple majority; a special majority in each House; a special majority plus ratification by at least half of the state legislatures.

cards.front_md: What is a **simple majority**?
cards.back_md: More than half of the members present and voting.

cards.front_md: What is a **special majority**?
cards.back_md: A majority of the total membership of the House and two thirds of the members present and voting.

cards.front_md: Which two matters are changed by a simple majority?
cards.back_md: Forming new states (Article 3) and creating or abolishing a Legislative Council (Article 169).

cards.front_md: Which provisions are amended by the special majority alone?
cards.back_md: Most provisions, including the Fundamental Rights.

cards.front_md: What is **ratification**?
cards.back_md: Formal approval of an amendment by the state legislatures; at least half must ratify a federal amendment.

cards.front_md: Name three matters that need ratification by the states
cards.back_md: For example the election of the President, the Seventh Schedule lists and the representation of states in Parliament.

cards.front_md: Where can an amendment bill be introduced?
cards.back_md: In either House of Parliament.

cards.front_md: Is there a joint sitting for an amendment bill?
cards.back_md: No: each House must pass it on its own.

cards.front_md: Who must assent to an amendment bill, and since when is it obligatory?
cards.back_md: The President; the 24th Amendment (1971) made assent obligatory.

cards.front_md: How many amendments have been made?
cards.back_md: More than one hundred; the 106th, in 2023, is the latest as of 2024.

questions.stem_md: A constitution written by one generation has to serve later generations as well. What is the main reason for giving it a procedure of amendment?

options.text_md: So that every new government can rewrite it at will
So that it can adapt to new needs and still stay stable and respected
So that courts no longer have to interpret it
So that it can never be changed under any circumstances

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** So that it can adapt to new needs and still stay stable and respected. An amendment procedure lets a constitution change with the times while making change deliberate and difficult enough to protect stability. Rewriting it at will would destroy stability, an amendment procedure does not remove the role of courts, and a constitution that can never change would fall behind new needs.

questions.stem_md: Which Article of the Constitution lays down the procedure for amending the Constitution?

options.text_md: Article 356
Article 280
Article 248
Article 368

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Article 368. Article 368 deals with the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution and the procedure for doing so. Article 356 is about President's Rule in a state, Article 280 about the Finance Commission and Article 248 about residuary powers of legislation.

questions.stem_md: Parliament passes a bill under Article 3 that separates some districts of the imagined state of Merivia to form a new state called Tarnia. Which statement about the majority and the procedure is correct?

options.text_md: A simple majority in each House is enough, and the change is not counted as an amendment under Article 368
A special majority and ratification by half of the state legislatures are needed, as for every constitutional change
Two thirds of the members of each House must vote for it, as for an amendment under Article 368
The Merivia legislature must approve the bill by a special majority before it can pass

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A simple majority in each House is enough, and the change is not counted as an amendment under Article 368. Forming a new state under Article 3 is done by an ordinary law of Parliament, passed by a simple majority, and is technically not an amendment under Article 368. The other options wrongly apply the procedures of Article 368, or give the state legislature a binding approval that Article 3 does not provide.

questions.stem_md: The imagined 147th Amendment Bill of the Harbour Road School project would change the powers of the High Courts. Which procedure must it follow, and why?

options.text_md: A simple majority in each House, because it changes no Fundamental Right
A special majority in each House alone, because only the Fundamental Rights need a special majority
A special majority in each House plus ratification by at least half of the state legislatures, because it changes a provision concerning the High Courts, which affects the federal structure
A special majority in each House plus approval by every state legislature, because any change to courts needs every state

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A special majority in each House plus ratification by at least half of the state legislatures, because it changes a provision concerning the High Courts, which affects the federal structure. The Supreme Court and the High Courts are among the matters that need ratification by at least half of the state legislatures after the special majority, since they touch the federal structure. A simple majority is the route for ordinary laws such as those under Article 3, a special majority alone is used for provisions such as the Fundamental Rights, and approval by every state is not part of the procedure.

questions.stem_md: The imagined 140th Amendment Bill, which would change a Fundamental Right, is put to the vote in a House that has 540 members in total. Of the 360 members present and voting, 270 vote for the bill. What is the result?

options.text_md: The bill passes, because 270 is more than two thirds of the 360 members voting
The bill passes, because 270 is a majority of the 360 members voting
The bill fails, because 270 is not a majority of the 540 members in total, even though it is more than two thirds of those voting
The bill fails, because every amendment of a Fundamental Right needs the vote of all the members

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** The bill fails, because 270 is not a majority of the 540 members in total, even though it is more than two thirds of those voting. More than half of 540 means at least 271 votes, and 270 falls one short, so the first condition is not met although 270 is above two thirds of 360, which is 240. The second option checks only one of the two conditions, the third applies the simple majority, and no amendment requires the vote of every member.

questions.stem_md: The imagined 141st Amendment Bill proposes to move a subject from the State List to the Union List of the Seventh Schedule. After it passes each House by the special majority, which further step is required before the amendment takes effect?

options.text_md: Ratification by the legislatures of at least half of the states, and then the assent of the President
Ratification by the legislatures of every state, with no exception
A referendum among all the voters of the country
No further step, because the President alone completes the amendment

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Ratification by the legislatures of at least half of the states, and then the assent of the President. A change to the lists of the Seventh Schedule affects the federal structure, so half of the state legislatures must ratify it before the President assents. A requirement that every state ratify, or a nationwide referendum, is not part of the procedure, and the President's assent alone is not enough for a federal provision.

questions.stem_md: The imagined 142nd Amendment Bill proposes to widen the scope of one of the Fundamental Rights. As commonly taught, which procedure applies to it?

options.text_md: A simple majority in each House, as for any ordinary law
A special majority in each House, plus ratification by at least half of the state legislatures
Approval by the Supreme Court before the bill is introduced
A special majority in each House, with no need for ratification by the states

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A special majority in each House, with no need for ratification by the states. Fundamental Rights are among the provisions amended by the special majority alone, since they do not concern the federal structure. An ordinary majority is too little, ratification by the states is reserved for federal provisions, and the Court does not approve a bill before it is introduced.

questions.stem_md: The imagined 144th Amendment Bill is passed by the Lok Sabha with the special majority, but the Rajya Sabha rejects it. A member proposes that a joint sitting of both Houses should decide the matter. What is the position?

options.text_md: A joint sitting can be held, and a simple majority of the joint sitting passes the bill
A joint sitting is not available for an amendment bill, so the bill cannot pass without the Rajya Sabha
The Lok Sabha vote alone is enough, since it is the House of the people
The President may pass the bill on the advice of the Lok Sabha alone

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A joint sitting is not available for an amendment bill, so the bill cannot pass without the Rajya Sabha. There is no joint sitting for an amendment bill, and each House must pass it by the special majority, so the rejection by the Rajya Sabha stops the bill. A joint sitting with a simple majority applies to some ordinary bills and not here, the Lok Sabha alone cannot pass an amendment, and the President cannot pass a bill.

questions.stem_md: Which amendment made it obligatory for the President to give assent to a constitution amendment bill that has been duly passed?

options.text_md: The 24th Amendment, 1971
The 15th Amendment, 1963
The 52nd Amendment, 1985
The 61st Amendment, 1988

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** The 24th Amendment, 1971. The 24th Amendment of 1971 made presidential assent obligatory. The 15th dealt with the retirement age of High Court judges, the 52nd with anti-defection and the 61st with the voting age.

questions.stem_md: Which statement about the number of amendments is correct as of 2024?

options.text_md: Fewer than fifty amendments have been made, and the 42nd is the latest
More than one hundred amendments have been made, and the 106th, passed in 2023, is the latest commonly counted
No amendment has been made since 1978
Exactly one hundred amendments have been made, all of them in 1950

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** More than one hundred amendments have been made, and the 106th, passed in 2023, is the latest commonly counted. By 2024 the Constitution had been amended more than a hundred times, the 106th Amendment of 2023 being the latest counted. The other options understate the number or give dates that are wrong.

questions.stem_md: A class at Harbour Road School sorts three imagined amendments of Tarnovia into the kinds taught in the chapter. Amendment X changes the month in which the state audit report is tabled. Amendment Y lowers the age for a local office after every party agreed on the text beforehand. Amendment Z is passed so that a new reading of a right by the courts no longer applies. Which sorting is correct?

options.text_md: X comes from political consensus, Y is technical or administrative, Z arises from differing interpretations
X arises from differing interpretations, Y is technical or administrative, Z comes from political consensus
X is technical or administrative, Y comes from political consensus, Z arises from differing interpretations of the judiciary and Parliament
X, Y and Z are all technical or administrative, since each changes only a detail

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** X is technical or administrative, Y comes from political consensus, Z arises from differing interpretations of the judiciary and Parliament. X adjusts a detail of timing, so it is technical or administrative. Y was agreed by all parties beforehand, which marks a consensus amendment. Z answers a court reading, so it arises from differing interpretations. The other sortings swap the kinds, and Y and Z are not details.

questions.stem_md: The imagined 150th Amendment Bill changes only the date by which the audit office of the imagined state of Pellara must file its yearly accounts, from 31 March to 30 June. As commonly grouped, this amendment is best described as

options.text_md: one arising from a disagreement between the judiciary and Parliament
one made through political consensus on a policy of national importance
one of the controversial amendments of the 1970s
technical or administrative, because it adjusts a detail without changing any policy

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** technical or administrative, because it adjusts a detail without changing any policy. A change of a filing date adjusts a detail and does not alter any principle, so it is technical or administrative. Nothing in the bill reverses a court reading, there is no policy that parties had to agree on, and it has no connection with the 1970s.

questions.stem_md: Before the imagined 146th Amendment Bill on the age for holding local office was introduced, leaders of every party in Parliament met and agreed on its text. Which kind of amendment is this likely to be, and which Indian amendment is a comparable example?

options.text_md: One arising from differing interpretations, comparable to the 15th Amendment (1963)
A technical amendment, comparable to the 42nd Amendment (1976)
A controversial amendment of the 1970s, comparable to the 73rd Amendment (1992)
One made through political consensus, comparable to the 61st Amendment (1988) on the voting age

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** One made through political consensus, comparable to the 61st Amendment (1988) on the voting age. A bill whose text all parties agree on beforehand is a consensus amendment, like the 61st Amendment, which lowered the voting age. The 15th Amendment was a technical change, the 42nd belongs to the 1970s group, and the 73rd was itself a consensus amendment on local government, not a controversial one.

questions.stem_md: Which words were added to the Preamble by the 42nd Amendment (1976)?

options.text_md: Sovereign, democratic and republic
Justice, liberty and equality
Socialist, secular and integrity
Federal, unitary and judicial

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Socialist, secular and integrity. The 42nd Amendment added the words socialist, secular and integrity to the Preamble. Sovereign, democratic and republic, and justice, liberty and equality, were already there, and federal, unitary and judicial are not Preamble terms.

questions.stem_md: Which description of the 42nd Amendment (1976) and the 44th Amendment (1978) is correct?

options.text_md: The 44th was passed first, and the 42nd later restored its provisions
The 42nd was passed during the national Emergency of 1975 to 1977, and the 44th restored several provisions that the 42nd had changed
Both were passed before the Constitution came into force
The 42nd left the Constitution unchanged, and the 44th added a Preamble

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The 42nd was passed during the national Emergency of 1975 to 1977, and the 44th restored several provisions that the 42nd had changed. The 42nd Amendment, passed during the Emergency, changed many parts of the Constitution, and the 44th Amendment of 1978 restored several of them. The order in the second option is reversed, the Constitution came into force in 1950, and the 42nd made many changes.

questions.stem_md: The 73rd and 74th Amendments, passed in 1992 through political consensus, dealt with

options.text_md: local government, in rural and urban areas
the voting age of citizens
defection by elected members
the retirement age of High Court judges

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** local government, in rural and urban areas. The 73rd Amendment concerned rural local government and the 74th urban local government. The voting age was changed by the 61st, defection by the 52nd, and the judges' retirement age by the 15th.

questions.stem_md: In the Golaknath case (1967), the Supreme Court held that

options.text_md: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution without any limit
Parliament cannot amend the Fundamental Rights
only the states can amend the Fundamental Rights
the Directive Principles can never be amended

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Parliament cannot amend the Fundamental Rights. The Court held in 1967 that Parliament could not amend the Fundamental Rights. The second option is the position that Parliament later asserted, the states have no such sole power, and nothing was said about the Directive Principles never being amended.

questions.stem_md: Parliament passed the 24th Amendment in 1971, after the Golaknath case. What did it assert?

options.text_md: That Parliament has no power to amend the Fundamental Rights
That only the Supreme Court can amend the Constitution
That the Constitution cannot be amended at all
That Parliament has power to amend any part of the Constitution, including the Fundamental Rights, and that the President must assent to an amendment bill

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** That Parliament has power to amend any part of the Constitution, including the Fundamental Rights, and that the President must assent to an amendment bill. The 24th Amendment asserted the amending power of Parliament over every part of the Constitution and made assent obligatory. The other options contradict this: they either deny the amending power, give it to the Court, or deny that it exists.

questions.stem_md: The Kesavananda Bharati case (1973) is best known for the principle that Parliament

options.text_md: can amend any part of the Constitution but cannot alter its basic structure
cannot amend any part of the Constitution at all
can amend any part of the Constitution without any limit
can amend only the Directive Principles

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** can amend any part of the Constitution but cannot alter its basic structure. The Court accepted a wide amending power but held that it stops short of altering the basic structure. The other options deny the amending power, ignore the limit, or restrict the power to the Directive Principles.

questions.stem_md: The imagined 143rd Amendment Act, passed by the special majority and ratified by the states, says that no court may examine whether any law is in accord with the Constitution. A petitioner challenges it. Under the basic structure doctrine, what may the Court do?

options.text_md: Refuse to hear the petition, because an amendment passed by the special majority can never be questioned
Declare that the Court itself has become the lawmaker for amendments
Examine whether the amendment alters a feature of the basic structure, such as judicial review, and strike it down if it does
Ask the Prime Minister to withdraw the Act

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Examine whether the amendment alters a feature of the basic structure, such as judicial review, and strike it down if it does. Judicial review has been identified as part of the basic structure, so the Court may test whether the Act alters it and may strike the Act down if it does. Passing by a special majority does not put an amendment beyond review, the Court does not become the lawmaker, and it does not ask a minister to withdraw an Act.

questions.stem_md: The imagined 148th Amendment Act, passed by the special majority and ratified by the states, lets the Union government dismiss any state government at will and take over all the legislative powers of the states permanently. Would it survive a challenge in the Supreme Court?

options.text_md: It must survive, because it was passed by the special majority and ratified by the states
It must survive, because the Court may never examine an amendment
It is likely to be struck down, because it destroys the federal character, a feature that the courts have listed as part of the basic structure
It is likely to be struck down, because every amendment that increases the Union government powers is invalid

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** It is likely to be struck down, because it destroys the federal character, a feature that the courts have listed as part of the basic structure. Federal character is among the features commonly listed in the basic structure, and an amendment that removes the powers of the states altogether alters it, so the Court may strike it down despite the special majority and ratification. Passing by the required majorities does not put an amendment beyond review, and not every change of the balance of powers touches the basic structure, so the last option is too wide.

questions.stem_md: The Minerva Mills case (1980) is mainly remembered because it

options.text_md: reaffirmed the basic structure doctrine and the balance between the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles
abolished the basic structure doctrine
created the Finance Commission
lowered the voting age to 18

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** reaffirmed the basic structure doctrine and the balance between the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles. Minerva Mills reaffirmed the doctrine of Kesavananda Bharati and the balance between the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles. It did not abolish the doctrine, and the Finance Commission and the voting age have no connection with it.

questions.stem_md: Why is the basic structure doctrine said to balance rigidity and flexibility?

options.text_md: Every provision can be changed by a simple majority
No provision can be changed at all
It lets the President amend the Constitution without Parliament
Most provisions can be amended to meet new needs, but the core features of the Constitution cannot be altered

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Most provisions can be amended to meet new needs, but the core features of the Constitution cannot be altered. The doctrine leaves the wide power to amend, which gives flexibility, and protects the core, which gives stability. A simple majority for everything would be pure flexibility, no change at all would be pure rigidity, and the President has no such amending power.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined country Quillan, the legislature may change any part of the written constitution by passing an ordinary law with a majority of the members voting. How would this constitution be described?

options.text_md: Rigid, since it is written
Flexible, since it is as easy to change as an ordinary law
Rigid, since a legislature is involved
Neither, since all constitutions are equally easy to change

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Flexible, since it is as easy to change as an ordinary law. A constitution that can be changed by the ordinary law-making process is flexible. Being written does not make a constitution rigid, the involvement of a legislature is true of both kinds, and constitutions do differ in how easily they can be changed.

questions.stem_md: The constitution of the imagined country Veldora can be changed only if three fifths of its voters approve in a national vote, and nine tenths of its provincial councils agree. This constitution is best described as

options.text_md: rigid, because change is made very difficult
flexible, because the voters are consulted
flexible, because it has provincial councils
unwritten, because voters are involved

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** rigid, because change is made very difficult. A procedure with several demanding conditions makes a constitution rigid. Consulting the voters or having provincial councils does not make it flexible, and the procedure says nothing about whether it is written.

questions.stem_md: A Harbour Road School student claims that the rigid constitution of the imagined country Veldora, amended only twice in sixty years, cannot be called a living document. Which judgment of this claim is best supported?

options.text_md: The claim is sound, because a constitution lives only through formal amendment
The claim is weak, because a constitution also lives through judicial interpretation and political conventions, so a rigid amendment procedure limits only one of the ways it can change
The claim is sound, because rigidity means that a constitution cannot adapt in any way
The claim is weak, because a rigid constitution is changed as easily as an ordinary law

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** The claim is weak, because a constitution also lives through judicial interpretation and political conventions, so a rigid amendment procedure limits only one of the ways it can change. Rigidity makes the formal route of amendment difficult, but courts can widen the meaning of rights and conventions can fill gaps, so the constitution can still adapt while keeping its core. The claim wrongly treats amendment as the only way of change. A rigid constitution is by definition hard to change, so the last option is false.

questions.stem_md: Street vendors of the imagined town of Halsey in Merivia are evicted without notice. Their petition says that courts have read the right to livelihood into the right to life and personal liberty under Article 21. Which way of keeping the Constitution alive does this illustrate?

options.text_md: A formal amendment under Article 368
An ordinary law passed by a simple majority
Judicial interpretation, which widens the meaning of a right without a formal amendment
A convention of the legislature

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Judicial interpretation, which widens the meaning of a right without a formal amendment. When courts read a wider meaning into an existing right, the Constitution develops through judicial interpretation, with no change of its text. No amendment bill or ordinary law is involved, and a convention is a practice of political actors, not a reading by courts.

questions.stem_md: The written constitution of the imagined country Pellara does not say whom its head of state must invite to form a government. For sixty years the head of state has invited the leader of the largest group in the legislature, and everyone expects this. This practice is an example of

options.text_md: an amendment under the written constitution
a court judgment
an ordinary law passed by the legislature
a political convention that fills a gap in the written text

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** a political convention that fills a gap in the written text. A long and accepted practice that fills a silence in the text is a convention, and conventions are one way in which political practice shapes how a constitution works. No amendment, judgment or law is mentioned in the description.

questions.stem_md: In the imagined country Pellara, a court reads a right to clean drinking water into the right to life. Ten years later the legislature passes an amendment that adds this right to the text. What does this sequence show?

options.text_md: The court's reading was invalid, so the legislature had to correct it
An amendment is never needed once a court has interpreted a right
Only the legislature can interpret a constitution
The judiciary and the legislature can both contribute to the growth of rights

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** The judiciary and the legislature can both contribute to the growth of rights. The court widened a right by interpretation and the legislature later gave it express form, so both institutions contributed. The amendment does not show that the reading was invalid, an amendment may still be useful after a reading, and courts do interpret constitutions.

questions.stem_md: A student has to give a balanced view on the basic structure doctrine. Which answer is balanced?

options.text_md: It is wrong, and nobody can defend it
It is perfect, and nobody can criticise it
Some argue that it gives judges too much power over the elected Parliament; others argue that it protects the core of the Constitution from being altered
It should not be discussed in a classroom

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** Some argue that it gives judges too much power over the elected Parliament; others argue that it protects the core of the Constitution from being altered. A balanced answer presents the reasons of both sides and lets the reader weigh them. The other options take one side without reasons or refuse to discuss the question.

questions.stem_md:

**Reason (R):** A special majority requires broad agreement, which makes a change of the Constitution more difficult than the passing of an ordinary law.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: the special majority is demanding on purpose, so that important provisions are not changed by a bare majority.

questions.stem_md:

**Reason (R):** The 24th Amendment (1971) asserted the power of Parliament to amend any part of the Constitution.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but R does not explain A: the 24th Amendment was a later response by Parliament to the position taken in the case, and not the reason for the Court's decision.

questions.stem_md:

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** A is false because the doctrine sets a limit on the amending power. R is true and states the limit, which contradicts A.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The 44th Amendment (1978) restored several provisions that the 42nd Amendment (1976) had changed.

**Reason (R):** The 44th Amendment was passed before the 42nd Amendment.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (c)** A is true. R is false: the 42nd Amendment was passed in 1976 and the 44th in 1978, so the 44th came later.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A change in the representation of states in Parliament needs ratification by at least half of the state legislatures.

**Reason (R):** Amendments of the Fundamental Rights need a special majority in each House of Parliament.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** Both statements are true, but R does not explain A: state ratification is needed because the change affects the federal structure, and the procedure for Fundamental Rights does not account for it.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The formation of a new state under Article 3 is not counted as an amendment under Article 368.

**Reason (R):** Article 3 allows Parliament to form new states by an ordinary law passed by a simple majority.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** Both are true, and R explains A: since Article 3 itself provides for an ordinary law, the change is made outside the procedure of Article 368.

questions.stem_md: Every change in the Constitution, including the creation of a new state, must be made by a special majority under Article 368.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** Some changes, such as the formation of new states under Article 3 and the creation or abolition of a Legislative Council under Article 169, are made by an ordinary law and are technically not amendments under Article 368.

questions.stem_md: The features that form the basic structure of the Constitution are not given in one fixed list in the text; the courts have identified them over time.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **True.** The doctrine was stated in Kesavananda Bharati, and the courts have since identified features, such as judicial review and the federal character, case by case.

questions.stem_md: The Minerva Mills case (1980) abolished the basic structure doctrine.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: **False.** It reaffirmed the doctrine and the balance between the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles.

questions.stem_md: What are technical or administrative amendments? Give one example.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and one example.

answer.model_answer_md: **Technical or administrative amendments** change a detail without altering the policy of the Constitution. For example, the **15th Amendment (1963)** raised the retirement age of **High Court judges from 60 to 62**.

marking_scheme.step: Change of a detail without altering a policy
Example: the 15th Amendment, retirement age of High Court judges raised from 60 to 62

questions.stem_md: Why are changes under Article 3 and Article 169 described as not amendments under Article 368 in the strict sense? Give the two matters.
questions.solution_md: The ordinary law and the two matters.

answer.model_answer_md: These changes are made by an **ordinary law of Parliament passed by a simple majority**, and not by the procedure of Article 368. **Article 3** deals with the **formation of new states**, and **Article 169** with creating or abolishing a **Legislative Council**.

marking_scheme.step: Made by an ordinary law with a simple majority

questions.stem_md: What did the Supreme Court hold in the Golaknath case (1967), and how did Parliament respond in 1971?
questions.solution_md: The holding and the response.

answer.model_answer_md: In **Golaknath (1967)** the Court held that **Parliament cannot amend the Fundamental Rights**. In **1971**, through the **24th Amendment**, Parliament **asserted its power to amend any part** of the Constitution.

marking_scheme.step: Golaknath: Parliament cannot amend the Fundamental Rights
24th Amendment (1971): Parliament asserted the power to amend any part

questions.stem_md: State the principle laid down in the Kesavananda Bharati case (1973).
questions.solution_md: The wide power and its limit.

answer.model_answer_md: In **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** the Supreme Court held that Parliament can **amend any part of the Constitution**, including the Fundamental Rights, but it **cannot alter the basic structure** of the Constitution. This is the **basic structure doctrine**.

marking_scheme.step: Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution
It cannot alter the basic structure

questions.stem_md: Name the case of 1980 that reaffirmed the basic structure doctrine and state what it stressed.
questions.solution_md: The name of the case and the balance.

answer.model_answer_md: The **Minerva Mills case (1980)** reaffirmed the **basic structure doctrine**. It stressed the **balance between the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles**, which the Constitution holds together.

marking_scheme.step: Balance between the Fundamental Rights and the Directive Principles

questions.stem_md: Why is the Constitution called a living document?
questions.solution_md: Growth through several routes with a stable core.

answer.model_answer_md: The Constitution is called a **living document** because it **keeps growing with society**. It changes through **formal amendments**, through the **interpretation of the courts** and through **political practice**, and yet it **keeps its core features**.

marking_scheme.step: It grows and adapts with society
Through amendment, interpretation and practice, keeping its core

questions.stem_md: Give one example of how judicial interpretation has widened rights without any amendment of the text.
questions.solution_md: An example from Article 21.

answer.model_answer_md: The courts have read many rights into **Article 21**, the right to **life and personal liberty**. For example, they have read in the **right to livelihood** and the **right to privacy**, so the rights grew **without any change in the wording**.

marking_scheme.step: Courts have read rights, such as livelihood or privacy, into Article 21
The rights widened without changing the text

questions.stem_md: How do political practice and conventions help a constitution to change? Give an imagined example.
questions.solution_md: Meaning of a convention and an imagined example.

answer.model_answer_md: **Conventions** are accepted practices that are **not written** in the constitution but guide how it works. For example, in imagined Pellara the head of state always **invites the leader of the largest group** to form a government, so the **practice changes how the text works**.

marking_scheme.step: Accepted practices that guide how the constitution works
An example of a practice filling a gap in the text

questions.stem_md: Describe the three ways in which the Constitution can be changed, as commonly taught.
questions.solution_md: Three ways, each with its use.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. By a **simple majority of Parliament**, as in forming new states under Article 3.
2. By a **special majority in each House**, for most provisions, including the Fundamental Rights.
3. By a **special majority plus ratification by at least half of the state legislatures**, for provisions that affect the federal structure.

marking_scheme.step: Special majority plus ratification by half of the state legislatures

questions.stem_md: Name any three matters on which an amendment needs ratification by the state legislatures, and say why states are involved.
questions.solution_md: Three matters and the federal reason.

answer.model_answer_md: Ratification is needed for matters such as the **election of the President**, the **Supreme Court and High Courts**, the **lists of the Seventh Schedule**, the **representation of states in Parliament** and **Article 368** itself. States are involved because these matters touch the **federal structure**.

marking_scheme.step: Any three matters, such as the election of the President or the Seventh Schedule lists
They affect the federal structure, so states must agree

questions.stem_md: Name three kinds of amendments, with one example for each.
questions.solution_md: Three kinds with examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Technical or administrative:** the 15th Amendment (1963) raised the retirement age of High Court judges.
2. **Political consensus:** the 52nd Amendment (1985) on anti-defection, or the 61st Amendment (1988) lowering the voting age.
3. **Differing interpretations** of the judiciary and Parliament, for example over property and the Fundamental Rights.

marking_scheme.step: Technical or administrative, with an example

questions.stem_md: State three facts about the 42nd Amendment (1976) and the 44th Amendment (1978).
questions.solution_md: Three accurate facts about the two Amendments.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **42nd Amendment** was passed during the **national Emergency (1975 to 1977)** and changed many parts of the Constitution.
2. It added the words **socialist, secular and integrity** to the Preamble, and the **Fundamental Duties**.
3. The **44th Amendment (1978)** restored several provisions.

marking_scheme.step: 42nd Amendment passed during the Emergency, with many changes
Words added to the Preamble; Fundamental Duties

questions.stem_md: What is the basic structure of the Constitution? Name any four features that the courts have identified, for example.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and four features.

answer.model_answer_md: The **basic structure** is the set of **core features** of the Constitution that Parliament **cannot alter** even by amendment. The courts have identified, for example, the **supremacy of the Constitution**, the **democratic form of government**, **judicial review** and the **federal character**.

marking_scheme.step: Core features that cannot be altered by amendment

questions.stem_md: Explain how the basic structure doctrine balances rigidity and flexibility, and limits the amending power.
questions.solution_md: Flexibility, stability and the limit.

answer.model_answer_md: The doctrine leaves Parliament a **wide power to amend** any provision, which gives the Constitution **flexibility** to meet new needs. It also **protects the core** features, which gives the Constitution **stability** and keeps it from being changed beyond recognition. In this way the doctrine **limits the amending power**, so that no amendment can **alter the basic structure**, even when it has the special majority.

marking_scheme.step: Wide power to amend gives flexibility
Protection of core features gives stability

questions.stem_md: Present the two views on the basic structure doctrine, giving one reason for each.
questions.solution_md: Both views with reasons.

answer.model_answer_md: Some argue that the doctrine gives **judges too much power**, since judges are not elected and can strike down an amendment passed by the elected Parliament. Others argue that it **guards the core** features against a majority of the moment. A student can weigh the reasons of both.

marking_scheme.step: View that judges have too much power, with a reason
View that the doctrine protects the core, with a reason
Both views presented without taking a side without reasons

questions.stem_md: Explain how Parliament and the judiciary have together contributed to the growth of the Constitution.
questions.solution_md: Amendment, interpretation and the combined effect.

answer.model_answer_md: Parliament changes the text through **amendments** under Article 368. The judiciary **interprets** the text, for example by reading many rights into **Article 21**, and has stated the **basic structure** limit. Their contributions **together** let the Constitution **grow** while it **keeps its core**.

marking_scheme.step: Parliament changes the text by amendments
The judiciary interprets and sets the basic structure limit
Together the Constitution grows and keeps its core

questions.stem_md: Explain the procedure for amending the Constitution, with the three ways in which it can be changed.
questions.solution_md: The Article, three ways and the other rules.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Article 368** lays down the procedure, which balances **rigidity and flexibility**.
2. Some matters, such as new states under **Article 3**, are changed by an **ordinary law with a simple majority**.
3. Most provisions need a **special majority in each House**: a majority of the total membership and two thirds of those present and voting.
4. Federal matters need the special majority **plus ratification by at least half of the state legislatures**.
5. A bill can start in **either House**, there is **no joint sitting**, and the **President must assent**.

marking_scheme.step: Article 368 and the balance between rigidity and flexibility
Special majority in each House, defined
Special majority plus ratification by states, for federal matters
Either House, no joint sitting, obligatory assent

questions.stem_md: Describe the kinds of amendments made to the Constitution, giving an example of each.
questions.solution_md: The number and four kinds with examples.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. Over **a hundred amendments** have been made, the 106th in 2023 being the latest as of 2024.
2. **Technical or administrative:** the **15th Amendment (1963)** raised the retirement age of High Court judges from 60 to 62.
3. **Differing interpretations** of the judiciary and Parliament, for example over **property and the Fundamental Rights**.
4. **Political consensus:** the **52nd (1985)** on anti-defection, the **61st (1988)** on the voting age of 18, and the **73rd and 74th (1992)** on local government.
5. **Controversial amendments of the 1970s**, such as the **42nd (1976)**.

marking_scheme.step: More than a hundred amendments, with a dated note
Technical or administrative, with an example

questions.stem_md: Describe the 42nd Amendment (1976) and the 44th Amendment (1978) and say why such amendments are studied as a separate group.
questions.solution_md: Facts of both, and the reason for studying them together.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The **42nd Amendment (1976)** was passed during the **national Emergency (1975 to 1977)** and changed many parts of the Constitution.
2. It added **socialist, secular and integrity** to the Preamble and added the **Fundamental Duties**.
3. The **44th Amendment (1978)** **restored several provisions** that the 42nd had changed.
4. They are studied as a group because a **single amendment changed many parts** and was then partly reversed.
5. They show how **amending power is used** and why the limits on it matter.

marking_scheme.step: 42nd Amendment passed during the Emergency, changing many parts
Words added to the Preamble and the Fundamental Duties
Why they form a group: wide changes, then reversal
Link with the limits on the amending power

questions.stem_md: Trace the development of the basic structure doctrine from the Golaknath case to the Minerva Mills case, and list the features commonly identified as part of the basic structure.
questions.solution_md: Four steps in order and the features.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. In **Golaknath (1967)** the Court held that Parliament **cannot amend the Fundamental Rights**.
2. The **24th Amendment (1971)** asserted that Parliament can **amend any part** of the Constitution.
3. In **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** the Court held that Parliament can amend any part but **cannot alter the basic structure**.
4. **Minerva Mills (1980)** **reaffirmed** the doctrine.
5. Features identified, for example, are the **supremacy of the Constitution**, the **democratic and republican form of government**, **secular character**, **separation of powers**, **federal character**, **judicial review** and the **rule of law**.

marking_scheme.step: Kesavananda Bharati 1973: the basic structure limit
Features identified, for example, by the courts

questions.stem_md: Examine the significance of the basic structure doctrine. Does it balance rigidity and flexibility? Give both views.
questions.solution_md: Balance, the limit and both views.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. The doctrine lets Parliament **amend any part**, which gives **flexibility**.
2. It forbids altering the **basic structure**, which gives **stability** and protects the core.
3. In this way it **limits the amending power** and balances **rigidity and flexibility**.
4. **Some argue** that it gives **judges too much power**, since they are not elected.
5. **Others argue** that it **guards the core** features against a majority of the moment.

marking_scheme.step: Protection of the core gives stability
View that judges gain too much power
View that the doctrine protects the core

questions.stem_md: Explain why the Constitution is called a living document, with the contribution of Parliament, the judiciary and political practice.
questions.solution_md: Meaning and three contributions.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. A **living document** keeps growing with society and yet **keeps its core**.
2. **Parliament** changes the text by **amendments** under Article 368.
3. The **judiciary** has widened rights by **interpretation**: the courts have read many rights into **Article 21**, such as the **right to livelihood** and the **right to privacy**.
4. **Political practice and conventions** also change how the Constitution works.
5. These contributions work **together**, and the **basic structure** keeps the core stable.

marking_scheme.step: Judicial interpretation, with an example from Article 21
They work together; the core is kept
